topics.title: FDA recall

facts.t: FDA Class I: “a reasonable probability” that using the product “will cause serious adverse health consequences or death.”
FDA Class II: the product “may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences,” or serious harm is remote.
FDA Class III: using the product “is not likely to cause adverse health consequences.”
Each FDA recall record names the firm that recalled and which products, sizes, lots or stores it covers.

not_known: A recall on record does not mean the bottle you have was affected: check the lot, size or store in the record.

facts.t: Aerosol spray sunscreens are among the products FDA lists as recalled for benzene contamination.
Under FDA labeling rules, “Broad Spectrum” means the product passed a test for UVA protection in addition to UVB.
Sunscreens that are not Broad Spectrum, or are below SPF 15, must carry the warning: “This product has been shown only to help prevent sunburn, not skin cancer or early skin aging.”
FDA: choose a broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of at least 15.
The CDC: SPF 15 or higher, broad spectrum, every 2 hours.
The AAP: at least SPF 15 “(up to SPF 50)”; “an SPF of 15 or 30 should be fine for most people.”
The American Academy of Dermatology recommends SPF 30 or higher.
Health Canada recommends SPF 30 or higher.
FDA has proposed (not finalized) that the maximum labeled SPF be 60+.

topics.title: Mineral or chemical UV filters

facts.t: The AAP's environmental health page says: “Mineral-based sunscreen (e.g., zinc oxide) is preferable to chemical-based sunscreen (e.g., oxybenzone).”
The AAP's 2021 safety tips say: “If possible, choose a sunscreen with the mineral ingredients zinc oxide or titanium dioxide.”
In 2021 FDA proposed (still not final) that zinc oxide and titanium dioxide are generally recognized as safe and effective at up to 25%.
For 12 older chemical filters, FDA proposed in 2021 that more safety data are needed; FDA says this is not a conclusion that they are unsafe.

In an FDA study in healthy adults who applied sunscreen to most of the body, six chemical filters (avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate, octinoxate) reached blood levels above the point at which FDA asks for further safety studies, after one application. The authors said this does not mean people should stop using sunscreen.

other_side.t: The AAD: “the science doesn't show that any sunscreen ingredients currently available in the U.S. are harmful to human health.”
FDA: “The fact that an ingredient is absorbed through the skin and into the body does not mean the ingredient is unsafe.”
The AAD says any of these sunscreens can protect you if it is broad spectrum, water resistant and SPF 30 or higher.
The AAP: “using any sunscreen is better than not using sunscreen at all.”

not_known: FDA's absorption studies were done in adults; we found no comparable study in children.

facts.t: FDA: spray sunscreens “should never be applied directly to your face.”
The AAD advises never spraying around the face or mouth or into the wind, to avoid inhaling it.
A pediatric dermatologist writing on the AAP's site says spray propellants “should not be inhaled by babies and children.”
FDA lists aerosol sunscreens among products recalled for benzene contamination; FDA says benzene is not usually used to make drugs, so it appears as a contaminant.
In the EU, nano zinc oxide may not be used in applications that could expose the user's lungs by inhalation.
The same EU condition applies to nano titanium dioxide.

other_side.t: FDA's 2021 proposal would keep sprays as an allowed sunscreen form, subject to testing and labeling requirements.

facts.t: US sunscreen labeling rules require the directions to say “children under 6 months of age: Ask a doctor.”
FDA: “Sunscreen is not recommended for infants under six months old.”
FDA's infant page adds that “the best sun protection for these infants is to stay in the shade.”
The AAP allows sunscreen on small areas such as the face if clothing and shade are not available.
Health Canada: “Do not put sunscreen on babies less than 6 months of age.”
“AAP does not recommend products that combine sunscreen with DEET.”
The AAD does not recommend sunscreen with insect repellent either.
Health Canada says sunscreen and insect repellent can be used safely together as separate products: apply the sunscreen first, then the repellent.
FDA issued a final order in September 2026 that sunscreens with PABA or trolamine salicylate as actives are not generally recognized as safe and effective; it takes effect in September 2027.
FDA allows “Water Resistant (40 minutes)” or “(80 minutes)” only after a set water test.
FDA: reapply at least every two hours, and more often if you're sweating or swimming.
The AAP advises reapplying every 2 hours and after swimming, sweating or drying off with a towel.
The AAP: “If possible, avoid the sunscreen ingredient oxybenzone because of concerns about mild hormonal properties.”
The EU limits oxybenzone to 6% in face, hand and lip products (not sprays) and 2.2% in body products, including sprays.
Hawaii has banned the sale of sunscreens containing oxybenzone (or octinoxate) without a prescription since January 1, 2021, citing harm to coral reefs.

other_side.t: The EU scientific committee found oxybenzone safe within those limits (6% face, hand and lip; 2.2% body).
The AAD: “the science doesn't show that any sunscreen ingredients currently available in the U.S. are harmful to human health.”
FDA: absorption into the body “does not mean the ingredient is unsafe.”

facts.t: The EU allows homosalate only in face products (not propellant sprays), up to 7.34%.
That limit followed the EU scientific committee's opinion that homosalate is safe up to 7.34% in face cream and pump spray.
The US allows up to 15%.
Homosalate reached blood levels above FDA's further-testing threshold in an FDA study in healthy adults.

other_side.t: FDA says its 2021 proposal that more data are needed for homosalate and other filters “does not represent a conclusion by the FDA” that they are unsafe.

topics.title: Octocrylene

facts.t: A 2021 study found benzophenone in the octocrylene-containing sunscreens and skin-care products it tested, and levels rose after an accelerated-aging test.
California lists benzophenone under Proposition 65 as a chemical known to cause cancer.
EU law requires benzophenone from octocrylene to be kept at trace levels.
In a 2025 safety review, Australia's TGA recommended limiting benzophenone in sunscreens to 383 ppm; this is a recommendation, not yet a final rule.

other_side.t: The EU scientific committee found octocrylene safe as a UV filter up to 10%.

not_known: We found no study measuring how much benzophenone a child's skin absorbs from an aged sunscreen, or whether that amount causes harm.

facts.t: Hawaii bans the sale of sunscreens containing oxybenzone or octinoxate without a prescription (Act 104, from January 1, 2021), citing harm to coral reefs.
Maui County bans the sale, distribution and use of non-mineral sunscreens without a prescription, from October 1, 2022.
FDA: “there are no FDA-approved or otherwise legally marketed OTC skin lightening products.”
FDA says over-the-counter hydroquinone products are deemed new drugs and are misbranded, and had to come off the market by September 23, 2020 unless FDA approved them.
FDA has received reports of serious side effects, including skin rashes, facial swelling and ochronosis, a skin discoloration that may be permanent.
The American Academy of Dermatology recommends SPF 30 or higher.
The AAP: at least SPF 15 “(up to SPF 50)”; “an SPF of 15 or 30 should be fine for most people.”
FDA: choose a broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of at least 15.

topics.title: Legal limits for UV filters

facts.t: FDA's sunscreen monograph lists the active ingredients (UV filters) an over-the-counter sunscreen may use, each with a maximum strength.
EU law lists the UV filters cosmetics may contain, each with a maximum concentration and any conditions of use.
Australia lists the ingredients sunscreens may contain, with their limits.

not_known: A limit in one country does not by itself show harm in another: each regulator sets limits on its own safety review.

topics.title: Ingredient list changed in the FDA filing

facts.t: DailyMed, the National Library of Medicine's database of FDA label filings, keeps a new version each time a label's filing changes.

not_known: This can be a correction to the filing, not a new formula.
A change in the filing does not show when the product on the shelf changed; older stock may still be sold, so check the tube.

topics.title: Same ingredient list as other labels

facts.t: These labels list the same active ingredients at the same strengths and the same inactive ingredients in the same order in their FDA filings.

not_known: A matching list does not show who makes the product, or that the amounts of each inactive ingredient are the same.

facts.t: The AAP recommends SPF at least 15 “(up to SPF 50)” and says more research is needed to test whether SPF above 50 offers extra protection.
FDA has proposed (not finalized) that the maximum labeled SPF be 60+.

other_side.t: The AAD recommends SPF 30 or higher; it says higher SPFs block slightly more UVB rays, but no sunscreen blocks 100%.

topics.title: Possible SPF booster listed as inactive

facts.t: FDA's sunscreen monograph lists the active ingredients (UV filters) an over-the-counter sunscreen may use.

A general FDA rule requires inactive ingredients in over-the-counter drugs to be safe in the amounts used and not to interfere with the product's effectiveness; it does not address SPF boosters specifically.
This product lists {names} among its inactive ingredients.
{status}
Hallstar, which makes butyloctyl salicylate, says it is “responsible for no more than 2 SPF units” at 5%.
Vantage sells tridecyl salicylate as a “sunscreen booster” for zinc oxide and titanium dioxide.

Butyloctyl and tridecyl salicylate are salicylates, the same chemical group as the approved filters octisalate and homosalate; the Cosmetic Ingredient Review assessed them together with octisalate (ethylhexyl salicylate).

other_side.t: A 2003 Cosmetic Ingredient Review assessment that covered butyloctyl and tridecyl salicylate found these ingredients safe in cosmetics when formulated to avoid skin irritation and increased sun sensitivity (or with directions for daily sun protection).
In 2025 the panel re-reviewed salicylic acid and 17 salicylates and found them safe as currently used in cosmetics when formulated to be non-irritating and non-sensitizing.
Hallstar says butyloctyl salicylate is “not a sunscreen active ingredient but rather a unique cosmetic ester”.

not_known: We found no published study measuring whether butyloctyl salicylate or tridecyl salicylate is absorbed into the body.
How much of this product's SPF, if any, comes from these ingredients cannot be told from the label.
We found no FDA rule, guidance or warning letter about SPF boosters.

facts.t: The EU banned 4-methylbenzylidene camphor in cosmetics: none could be newly sold from May 1, 2025 and none at all from May 1, 2026.
The EU scientific committee found sufficient evidence that it may act as an endocrine disruptor, and could not set a safe concentration because data on possible genotoxicity were insufficient.

other_side.t: Australia's 2023 sunscreen guidelines permitted it up to 4%.
Australia's TGA published a new safety review of it in September 2026.

facts.t: FDA approved bemotrizinol as a sunscreen active ingredient (up to 6%), effective August 9, 2026.
Data submitted with the application showed it is not readily absorbed through human skin.
US rules let companies list all fragrance components as one word, “Fragrance”.
FDA says some fragrance components may cause allergic reactions or sensitivities.
For children with eczema, the AAD advises fragrance-free rather than “unscented” products and a fragrance-free sunscreen.
The EU requires named fragrance allergens to be listed individually above 0.001% in leave-on products.
The 2022 US law MoCRA required FDA to propose a similar fragrance allergen labeling rule by June 29, 2024.
Trade press reported that FDA's July 2026 regulatory agenda projected that proposal for November 2026; it had not been published as of that report.
FDA says diethyl phthalate (DEP) appears to be the only phthalate still commonly used in cosmetics, and it may be part of an ingredient listed as “fragrance”.

other_side.t: FDA says it does not have evidence that phthalates as used in cosmetics pose a safety risk.

topics.title: Lavender or tea tree oil

facts.t: A 2007 report described three healthy boys whose breast growth started while using products containing lavender oil (in one case also tea tree oil) and stopped when the products were stopped.
NIEHS researchers found chemicals in these oils with estrogen-like or anti-androgen activity in cell tests; an NIEHS scientist described such effects in children as very rare.

other_side.t: A 2021 survey study of more than 550 children reported no link between lavender or tea tree oil use and hormone effects; it came from a research center that works with natural-products brands.

not_known: Case reports cannot show the oils caused it, and we found no established safe or unsafe amount.

facts.t: The EU has banned methylisothiazolinone in leave-on cosmetics since February 12, 2017, because no safe level for causing skin allergy was shown.
The EU has banned the MCI/MI mixture in leave-on cosmetics since 2015.
The EU requires products to be labeled “releases formaldehyde” when released formaldehyde exceeds 0.001%.
The EU bans propylparaben and butylparaben in leave-on products designed for the diaper area of children under 3, because a risk for babies under 6 months could not be excluded.

other_side.t: Outside diaper-area products for young children, EU law allows propyl- and butylparaben up to 0.14% combined, a limit set on the EU scientific committee's safety advice.
FDA: “At this time, we do not have information showing that parabens as they are used in cosmetics have an effect on human health.”

topics.title: Retinyl palmitate (vitamin A)

facts.t: In a 2012 government study, a cream with retinyl palmitate sped up skin tumors caused by simulated sunlight in hairless mice.
EU law adopted in 2024 caps vitamin A at 0.05% (retinol equivalent) in body lotion and 0.3% in other products, and requires the label “Contains Vitamin A. Consider your daily intake before use.”

other_side.t: The EU scientific committee found vitamin A safe in cosmetics at those limits, while noting that food and supplements alone may push the most-exposed 5% of people above the upper limit.

not_known: The study was in mice and did not draw conclusions about people; we found no FDA statement on retinyl palmitate in sunscreen.

topics.title: Food-derived ingredients

facts.t: NIH peanut allergy guidelines identify infants with severe eczema, egg allergy, or both as at highest risk of peanut allergy, and advise that, after evaluation, peanut-containing foods be introduced as early as 4 to 6 months.

A 2003 UK observational study found peanut-oil creams used on babies' rashes were associated with a higher risk of peanut allergy; the researchers said this needed confirmation and that parents should ask a doctor before changing creams.

other_side.t: FDA’s over-the-counter monograph lists colloidal oatmeal as a skin protectant active ingredient.
The National Eczema Association lists oat among ingredients that can help soothe eczema-prone skin.

not_known: The skin-exposure link comes from observational studies and is a hypothesis, not a proven cause. Refined oils may contain little protein; labels do not say.

topics.title: Citrus peel oil

facts.t: Furocoumarins, found naturally in some citrus oils such as bergamot and lime, can cause a skin reaction when the skin is then exposed to UVA light.
EU law requires furocoumarins to stay below 1 mg/kg in sun protection and bronzing products.

not_known: The label does not say whether this oil has had its furocoumarins removed.

facts.t: The AAD: “To prevent a flare due to sunscreen, use sunscreen that contains only these active ingredients: titanium dioxide, and/or zinc oxide.”
The same AAD page says the sunscreen should also be fragrance-free and broad-spectrum.
The AAD says sunscreens with titanium dioxide or zinc oxide are less likely to irritate a baby's sensitive skin.
The AAP's dermatology section advises mineral-based, broad-spectrum, alcohol- and fragrance-free sunscreen for sensitive areas.
The National Eczema Association's Seal considers only physical sunscreens containing titanium, zinc and iron, and requires products to be fragrance-free.

other_side.t: An AAP page on eczema and sports recommends a broad-spectrum, oil-free, water-resistant sunscreen of at least SPF 15, without specifying mineral filters.
DermNet NZ notes that many allergies to sunscreen products are caused by inactive ingredients, such as fragrances or preservatives, rather than the UV filter.

topics.title: On the National Eczema Association's exclusion list

facts.t: A product cannot carry the National Eczema Association's Seal if it contains any ingredient on its exclusion list, in any amount.
This product contains {names}.

other_side.t: The NEA says a product that works for one person may not work for another.

facts.t: A 2023 review in the journal Dermatitis names oxybenzone as the most frequently reported contact and photocontact allergen among UV filters.
The same review found no reports of allergic or photoallergic contact dermatitis to zinc oxide or titanium dioxide.
For people with allergy-prone skin, the AAD advises avoiding sunscreen with fragrance, parabens or oxybenzone.

other_side.t: Among 23,908 people referred for patch testing in North America, sunscreen was the source of an allergy for 0.9%.
Fragrance and vitamin E were among the allergens behind those sunscreen reactions, so the other ingredients matter too.

facts.t: An AAP page on eczema in teens lists alcohols such as ethanol among ingredients that may irritate the skin, and adds that each person may react differently or not at all.
The AAD lists alcohol among products to stop using for dry skin.
The American Contact Dermatitis Society named lanolin its 2023 Allergen of the Year; a review published with the designation lists children and people with eczema among higher-risk groups.
Among children referred for patch testing in a US registry, those with eczema reacted to lanolin more often than those without eczema.

other_side.t: The same review describes lanolin as a rare sensitizer in people with healthy skin.

facts.t: Among children referred for patch testing in a US registry, those with eczema reacted to cocamidopropyl betaine more often than those without eczema.

other_side.t: The Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel concluded in 2010 that it is safe in cosmetics when formulated to be non-sensitizing, and has linked sensitization concerns to manufacturing impurities (amidoamine and DMAPA).

facts.t: The American Contact Dermatitis Society named propylene glycol its 2018 Allergen of the Year; a systematic review calls it a weak sensitizer and an irritant.

other_side.t: Among 6,761 people with suspected contact dermatitis patch tested in Australia (2005-2020), 21 (0.31%) reacted to propylene glycol, and 9 of them had a reaction judged relevant.

facts.t: The AAD says skin injuries, including sunburn, can trigger a psoriasis flare near or at the injury, about 10 to 14 days later.
The AAD recommends broad-spectrum, SPF 30+, water-resistant sunscreen on uncovered skin that is free of psoriasis.
The National Psoriasis Foundation recommends fragrance-free moisturizers.
The National Psoriasis Foundation says the body may absorb too much salicylic acid if it is used over large areas of skin.
The AAD says salicylic acid applied before phototherapy can make UVB treatment less effective.
EU law does not allow salicylic acid in preparations for children under 3 (the only exception is shampoos, where it is used as a preservative).

topics.title: Common allergens in children

facts.t: Among 1,871 children referred for patch testing in North America (2001-2018), the most common relevant allergens were nickel (17.3%), hydroperoxides of linalool (7.8%), methylisothiazolinone (7.7%), cobalt (7.0%) and fragrance mix I (4.9%).

not_known: These figures come from children already referred for testing, so they are not population rates.

facts.t: FDA says there are no federal standards for the term “hypoallergenic”; it means whatever a company wants it to mean.
The EU scientific committee found phenoxyethanol safe as a preservative up to 1%, including for young children.

In 2019 France required most leave-on products with phenoxyethanol to carry a label against use on the diaper area of children aged 3 and under; its highest administrative court annulled that decision in 2022 for lack of legal basis.

topics.title: PEG and other ethoxylated ingredients

facts.t: FDA says these ingredients can carry trace 1,4-dioxane, a manufacturing byproduct it calls a potential human carcinogen.
New York limits 1,4-dioxane to 10 ppm in cosmetics and 1 ppm in personal care products; the state's guidance does not say whether over-the-counter sunscreens are covered.

other_side.t: FDA reports the EU committee considered trace levels of 10 ppm or less safe, and that levels have fallen over time.

not_known: A label cannot show whether any 1,4-dioxane is present.

facts.t: The US National Toxicology Program lists BHA as reasonably anticipated to be a human carcinogen, based on animal studies; it says human data are inadequate.
California lists BHA under Proposition 65 as a chemical known to cause cancer (since 1990).

other_side.t: In 2026 the EU scientific committee gave its opinion that BHA is safe on skin up to 0.07% in leave-on and rinse-off cosmetics; this is advice, not yet an EU legal limit.

facts.t: The EU scientific committee found BHT safe up to 0.8% in leave-on and rinse-off cosmetics (lower in mouthwash and toothpaste), a limit it set after considering concerns about BHT’s potential endocrine-disrupting properties.
FDA says talc can be contaminated with asbestos, a known cause of cancer when inhaled.
FDA proposed asbestos testing of talc cosmetics in 2024 and withdrew the proposal in November 2025, saying it will issue a new one.

WHO's cancer agency classified talc as probably carcinogenic (Group 2A) in 2024, citing limited evidence in humans for ovarian cancer (from studies of genital use), sufficient evidence in animals and strong mechanistic evidence; it said asbestos contamination could not be ruled out in the human studies. This rates hazard, not the risk from a given product.

other_side.t: Health Canada concluded most uses of talc are not a concern to human health; its concerns were breathing in loose powders and genital use.

topics.title: Petrolatum or mineral oil

facts.t: Germany's BfR found no health risk to be expected from highly refined (pharmaceutical-grade) mineral oils applied to the skin.
The AAD recommends petroleum jelly for babies' diaper rash.

not_known: US labels do not say whether the mineral oil or petrolatum is highly refined.

topics.title: Nano zinc oxide or titanium dioxide

facts.t: In its 2019 sunscreen proposal, FDA wrote that zinc oxide stays mainly in the outer dead layers of the skin, whatever its particle size.
The EU allows nano zinc oxide up to 25%, under conditions on purity and coating, but not in products that could expose the lungs by inhalation.
The EU allows nano titanium dioxide up to 25% under similar conditions, also not in products that could expose the lungs by inhalation.
California lists titanium dioxide under Proposition 65 only in the form of airborne, unbound particles of respirable size.
Australia's TGA concluded these nanoparticles are not likely to cause harm in sunscreens.

not_known: US labels are not required to say whether zinc oxide or titanium dioxide is nano-sized.
